questions: What exactly qualifies as a “key character” – is it any alphabetic letter, a specific set of characters, or something else?
How is “a part of a word” defined – does a preceding or following alphanumeric character make the last character part of a word, or are delimiters like spaces or punctuation considered?
Should the function treat Unicode letters (e.g., accented characters, non‑Latin scripts) as letters, or only ASCII A‑Z/a‑z?
If the input string ends with whitespace or other non‑visible characters, are those considered when determining the last character?
How should the function behave when the input string is empty or contains no characters at all?
Are surrogate pairs or combined grapheme clusters (e.g., emojis, characters formed by multiple code points) considered a single character for this check?
Does the presence of punctuation immediately before the last character affect whether it is considered “part of a word”?
Should the function raise an error for non‑string inputs, or coerce them to strings and then evaluate?
answers: "key character" is a substitution for "alphabetical character" -- it means any letter a-z/A-Z, exactly as in the original spec.

A word is a group of characters separated by spaces; the last character is 'part of a word' if it is not the sole character after the final space (i.e. the last space-delimited token has length > 1). This is a genuine but separate ambiguity from the 'key character' substitution.
